title: Moses Drawn from the Water
summary: A Levite woman hides her baby son, then places him in a papyrus basket among the reeds of the Nile, where Pharaoh's daughter finds him, pays his own mother to nurse him, and adopts him, naming him Moses. Grown, Moses kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew, is challenged by a fellow Hebrew, and flees from Pharaoh to Midian, where he defends the daughters of Reuel at a well, marries Zipporah, and has a son. Meanwhile the Israelites cry out under their slavery, and God hears, remembers his covenant, sees, and takes notice.
story: Pharaoh has just ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (1:22). This chapter answers that decree with a baby placed in the Nile and saved by it, and raised in Pharaoh's own house. It then leaps forward to Moses as a grown man. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:23 puts him at forty years old when he went out to his people, a figure Exodus itself does not give, and by Exodus 7:7 he will be eighty. His first attempt to help his people fails, and he ends up a shepherd in Midian, a foreigner with a son named for his exile. The chapter closes by turning from Moses to God. The long years of slavery continue, the old king dies, and the people's cry rises to God, who remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Everything is ready for the burning bush in Exodus 3.
historical:
Egypt's New Kingdom court raised and educated children from outside the royal family, including the children of foreign rulers brought to Egypt, alongside Egyptian princes. A Hebrew boy adopted by a king's daughter would have received the education of the Egyptian elite, which is how Stephen describes Moses, educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). His name fits that setting. Moses is most likely an Egyptian name from the word meaning born or son, found in royal names such as Thutmose and Ramesses. In Hebrew it sounds like the verb to draw out, which is the pun Pharaoh's daughter makes in verse 10.

Stories of a child set adrift and rescued circulated in the ancient Near East. The best known is the Legend of Sargon, known from copies of the first millennium BC, in which the mother of Sargon of Akkad places him in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and sets him in the river, where a water-drawer finds and raises him. Some scholars think Exodus uses a familiar motif; others note that the exposure of infants was common enough to produce similar stories independently. The differences are marked: Moses' mother acts to save him from a decree of death, and his rescuer is the daughter of the king who ordered it. Midian, where Moses flees, lay in northwest Arabia east of the Gulf of Aqaba; the Midianites were descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2).
cultural:
The basket was made of papyrus reeds and waterproofed with tar and pitch, the kind of materials used for Nile boats. Pharaoh's daughter bathing in the river with her attendants, and her decision to hire a Hebrew wet nurse, reflect ordinary practice; wet nursing by hired women was common, and weaning could come at two or three years of age. The irony would not have escaped an Israelite reader: Pharaoh's household pays Moses' own mother to raise the child Pharaoh ordered killed.

The scene at the well in Midian follows a pattern Israel knew from its ancestors. Abraham's servant found Rebekah at a well (Genesis 24), and Jacob met Rachel at a well (Genesis 29); in each case a stranger arrives, water is drawn, the young woman runs home, hospitality follows, and a marriage results. Moses fits the pattern, and like Jacob he waters a flock for women who have been wronged. The priest of Midian is called Reuel here and Jethro in 3:1, and Numbers 10:29 mentions Hobab son of Reuel. The Bible does not explain the names, and interpreters have suggested that one is a title, that the family used more than one name, or that Reuel was a clan head rather than Zipporah's father.
literary: Most of the people in the first half of the chapter are unnamed: a man of the house of Levi, a daughter of Levi, the child's sister, Pharaoh's daughter. The first name given is Moses, bestowed by an Egyptian princess. The basket is called by the same Hebrew word as Noah's ark (see the word note), linking this rescue through water with the first. The second half shows three scenes of Moses stepping in against injustice: an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, a Hebrew wronging a Hebrew, and shepherds driving off women at a well. The first ends in killing, the second in rejection with the words “Who made you ruler and judge over us?”, and the third in rescue and a home. The chapter's final paragraph (vv. 23-25) slows down and stacks four verbs with God as subject: God heard, God remembered, God saw, and God knew (translated took notice). After two chapters in which God is barely mentioned, the narrator makes plain that he has been attentive all along.

outline.t: Moses is born, hidden, and placed in the Nile
Pharaoh's daughter rescues and adopts him
Moses kills an Egyptian and flees Pharaoh
Moses in Midian: the well, Zipporah, and Gershom
Israel cries out and God remembers his covenant

doctrines.note: Pharaoh's river becomes Moses' rescue, Pharaoh's daughter becomes his protector, and Pharaoh's treasury pays for his nursing. God is not named in the story of Moses' birth, yet every turn serves his purpose. Providence here works through a mother's courage, a sister's quick thinking, and a princess's compassion.

God “remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (v. 24). The rescue of Israel rests on promises God made centuries earlier. To remember in Scripture is to act on a commitment, and this verse is the hinge on which the whole book turns from slavery to rescue.

The Israelites groaned and cried out under their slavery, and their cry rose to God (v. 23). The text does not say they addressed their cry to God, only that it reached him. The God of Exodus hears even inarticulate groaning, a truth Paul echoes when he speaks of the Spirit interceding with groans too deep for words (Romans 8:26).

words.note: Tevah, box or chest, the word for Moses' basket (vv. 3, 5). The only other place it appears in the Old Testament is the story of the flood, where it names Noah's ark. In both stories God preserves life through water that brings death to others, and the one saved in the ark becomes the beginning of something new.

Mashah, to draw out. Pharaoh's daughter explains the name Moses (Hebrew Mosheh) by saying, “I drew him out of the water” (v. 10). The name is probably Egyptian, but the Hebrew pun is deliberate, and the form of the name in Hebrew suggests the one who draws out. The boy drawn out of the water will draw Israel out through the sea.

Zakar, to remember. When God remembers (v. 24), it is never a matter of recovering forgotten information. It means turning to act on a relationship or a promise, as when God remembered Noah and the waters receded (Genesis 8:1). The word signals that rescue is about to begin.

christ: The New Testament reads Moses' early life as part of a pattern that leads to Christ. In Acts 7, Stephen dwells on the Hebrew's challenge in verse 14 and draws the lesson: Moses supposed his people would understand that God was using him to rescue them, but they did not, and the man they rejected was the one God sent to be their ruler and redeemer (Acts 7:25, 35). Stephen then accuses his hearers of resisting God as their fathers did, culminating in the rejection of Jesus (Acts 7:51-52). Hebrews says Moses refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing to suffer with God's people, and that he counted reproach for the sake of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:24-26). And the God who remembered his covenant in verse 24 is the God who, in Zechariah's song at the birth of John the Baptist, remembers his holy covenant in sending the Savior (Luke 1:72). The link is a pattern of rejected deliverers and a faithful God, completed in Christ.

hard.q: Was Moses right to kill the Egyptian?
hard.a:
The text reports the act without an explicit verdict, and readers have long disagreed. Some see it as a justified defense of a helpless man. The Egyptian was beating a Hebrew, perhaps to death, and the same Hebrew verb is used for the Egyptian's blows and for Moses' blow, suggesting that Moses answered violence with the force it deserved. Stephen in Acts 7:24-25 presents the act as Moses defending the oppressed and expecting his people to see that God was using him to save them, and Hebrews praises Moses' choice to side with God's people rather than enjoy Egypt's privileges.

Others read the details as a warning. Moses looked this way and that before striking (v. 12), which suggests secrecy rather than open justice. He acted on his own initiative, without any word from God, and his attempt at deliverance failed: his own people rejected him and he fled for his life. On this reading, the chapter shows sincere zeal that was not yet shaped by God's call, and it takes long years in the wilderness before Moses is sent. Both readings take seriously that Moses was right to side with the oppressed. They differ over whether his method was justice or a rash act that God later redeemed.

questions: Moses' first attempt to help his people came by his own hand and ended in failure and exile. What is the difference between zeal for justice and trusting God's call and timing?

God's purposes in this chapter move through women with little power: a mother, a sister, an Egyptian princess, seven shepherd daughters. Who are the unnoticed people through whom God has worked in your life?
The chapter ends with God hearing, remembering, seeing, and taking notice. What difference does it make to your own groaning that God is described this way?
